original_value: As robots move beyond manufacturing applications to less predictable environments, they can increasingly benefit, as animals do, from integrating sensing and control with the passive properties provided by particular combinations and arrangements of materials and mechanisms. This realization is partly responsible for the recent proliferation of soft and bioinspired robots. Tuned materials and mechanisms can provide several kinds of benefits, including energy storage and recovery, increased physical robustness, and decreased response time to sudden events. In addition, they may offer passive open-loop behaviors and responses to external changes in loading or environmental conditions. Collectively, these properties can also increase the stability of a robot as it interacts with the environment and allow the closed-loop controller to reduce the apparent degrees of freedom subject to control. The design of appropriate materials and mechanisms remains a challenging problem; bioinspiration, genetic algorithms, and numerical shape and materials optimization are all applicable. New multimaterial fabrication processes are also steadily increasing the range and magnitude of passive properties available for intrinsically responsive robots.

result.paraphrase: As robots move from manufacturing into less predictable settings, they can increasingly, like animals, profit from combining sensing and control with the passive properties produced by specific material and mechanism pairings and arrangements. This insight is partly behind the recent surge in soft and bioinspired robots. Carefully tuned materials and mechanisms can provide multiple advantages, including energy storage and recovery, greater physical robustness, and faster responses to sudden events. They can also enable passive open-loop behaviors and responses to changes in loading or environmental conditions. Together, these traits can improve a robot’s stability when interacting with its environment and let the closed-loop controller reduce the apparent degrees of freedom that must be controlled. Designing suitable materials and mechanisms remains difficult; bioinspiration, genetic algorithms, and numerical shape and materials optimization are all relevant approaches. Meanwhile, new multimaterial fabrication processes are steadily expanding the range and strength of passive properties available to intrinsically responsive robots.
